section_1.title: The Hook: The Prisoner's Dilemma
section_1.content: Introduce the problem: A warden forces two prisoners to play a game. A chessboard with 64 squares is filled with 64 coins (Heads/Tails). The warden hides a key under one square. One prisoner identifies the square; the other must guess which one it is to survive. How can they ensure survival with 100% certainty?
section_1.example: Visualize two characters, 'Alice' and 'Bob', standing on opposite sides of a giant 8x8 grid of glowing coins.

section_2.title: Prerequisite: The Parity Bit (Information Foundation)
section_2.content: Explain the concept of 'Parity'. Parity is the simplest form of error-detecting code. If we have a set of bits, the parity bit tells us if the count of '1's (Heads) is even or odd. This is the fundamental unit of information compression.
section_2.example: Show a row of 3 coins: [H, T, T]. If H=1 and T=0, the sum is 1 (odd). Adding a parity bit of 1 makes the total sum even. Graphical animation: A 'checksum' balance scale.

section_3.title: Mapping the Board to the Information Space
section_3.content: Apply the math: Assign a binary number (0-63) to each square. Treat the state of the 64 coins as a 64-bit string. Alice can calculate the parity of the current board state. By flipping exactly one coin, she can force the parity of any subset of squares to match the target secret square.
section_3.example: Visual overlay: An 8x8 grid where each square has a coordinate index. Alice performs a XOR summation of the binary indices of all 'Heads' coins.

section_4.title: The Solution: Communication through State Change
section_4.content: Alice communicates one bit of information by changing the parity of the entire board to point to the secret square index. Bob, seeing the new board configuration, calculates the parity and recovers the exact coordinate of the key.
section_4.example: A 2D animation showing the 'parity vector' pointing to the hidden key square as Alice flips one coin.

section_5.title: Conclusion: The Power of Information Theory
section_5.content: Reflect on how this bridges logic and information. We didn't 'guess'; we used the board as an information channel. This illustrates the principle of 'Zero-Knowledge Proofs' and Error Correction, which are vital for modern computer networks.
section_5.example: Final shot: Alice and Bob walking free, with the chessboard dissolving into binary code (1s and 0s) floating in the air.

from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(f"- {line}", font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 1.5 + j * 0.8
